title: The Dad Discount
logline: Mickey Aldrin's fifty-second board game is Pick-Up, a race across New York to collect your kid from school, and Marshall, who can't say no to anyone's dream, secretly bankrolls it with Lily's studio fund. Lily, who takes a hundred percent off anything her father promises, finds out from the IOU.

guests.name: Dot
guests.role: Owner of Dot's Games and Melons on Amsterdam for thirty years; has rejected all fifty-one of Mickey's games and keeps every one of them in a binder she reads aloud like scripture

guests.name: Renee
guests.role: A frazzled single mom who runs in for a birthday present while late for her own son's school pickup, and becomes the first person in history to buy a Mickey Aldrin game

facts.lily.job: kindergarten teacher; waits with the last kid at pickup and deals them in
facts.lily.childhood: last kid at the school gate for six years; a crossing guard taught her gin rummy
facts.lily.dad_rule: the Dad Discount: 100% off Mickey's promises (once gave him 90% off)
facts.mickey.games: 52 invented; Pick-Up, whose board loops to the dog track, is the only one sold
facts.mickey.wednesdays: came to Lily's school every Wednesday that year; lost every gin rummy hand
facts.lily.studio: Marshall gave her $1,500 studio fund to Mickey; his rummy losses paid it back
facts.marshall.slap_bet: refused Barney's $2,000 to buy back one slap; slap count unchanged
facts.mickey.store: Dot's Games and Melons on Amsterdam; Dot rejected his other 51 games

opens.note: Mickey has a sequel idea, Pick-Up Two: Detention; Marshall said no
Barney has Renee's number from the Pick-Up sale; she said to call after eight

scenes.summary: Cold open. Mickey pitches Pick-Up to Marshall: a race across New York to get your kid before the school closes, with suspiciously specific obstacle cards. He needs $1,500. Marshall caves and hands over the envelope marked Lily's studio fund, P.S. included. Mickey asks when he has ever let his little girl down; Marshall earnestly starts to list.

beats.line: Lily's father, Mickey Aldrin, had invented fifty-one board games and sold exactly zero.
Marshall. It's 3:14. School lets out at 3:15. And you are stuck on the wrong side of Queens.
Oh, no. Queens? Where every street is called Thirty-Seventh something?
Doesn't matter. Your kid is waiting. This is Pick-Up. The after-school race across New York.
I'm sweating, Mickey. I don't even have a kid, and I'm sweating.
Every turn, you draw a card. Your car gets towed from the dog track. Again.
You stop for one quick beer with Gary. It is now Tuesday.
Who are these dads?
Ordinary dads, Marshall.
All I need is fifteen hundred dollars for two hundred copies. Dot's Games gives me a launch Saturday.
Mickey, I'd love to. But the only money we have is Lily's—
I'm not asking Lily, son. I'm asking the one guy in this family who still believes in me.
Lily's studio fund. Do not touch. This means you, Marshall.
P.S. I mean it, Marshmallow.
Relax. When have I ever let my little girl down?
Well, there was her eighth birthday, and then the Christmas with the—
Rhetorical! Saturday, three o'clock!

scenes.summary: The booth. Lily announces the new game and introduces the Dad Discount (runner 1). Barney briefly loves a game called Pick-Up. Lily was the last kid at the gate for six years; now she's the teacher who waits with the last kid, and hustles them at gin rummy. Marshall, carrying the secret, sweats.

beats.line: My dad has a new game called Pick-Up. And this time, quote, it's going in stores.
So I did what I always do. I applied the Dad Discount. Whatever he promises, a hundred percent off.
I'll be at your recital, Pumpkin. Hundred percent off. You can't be disappointed by zero. It's very freeing.
That's the saddest coupon I've ever heard.
Back up. A board game called Pick-Up? Lily, I have badly misjudged your father.
It's about after-school pickup. You race across the city to get your kid.
Why would anyone race toward a child?
Which is hilarious, because he never picked me up once. I was the last kid at that gate for six years.
The crossing guard taught me gin rummy. By fifth grade I was taking the janitor for twelve bucks a week.
Now I'm the teacher who waits with whoever's last. I deal them in.
You hustle five-year-olds?
I let them win till they're six.
But what if this time, hypothetically, somebody believed in him? With money?
Marshall, why are you sweating?
Wings.
We didn't order wings.
That's how hot they are.

scenes.summary: The playtest. Robin plays to win, Barney finds the divorcee card, Ted asks why the kid piece holds a paintbrush. Mickey promises Lily the studio he is literally spending; Lily applies the Dad Discount (runner 2). Mickey nearly thanks his executive producer, Mar-; Marshall turns it into Marvelous Ted.

beats.line: Ted. Roll the dice, or I roll you.
I'm reading the rules, Robin. Somebody should read the rules.
Nobody in Canada reads the rules. Board games are how we survive February.
Barney, draw a card.
Your ex-wife is waiting at the curb. She looks furious.
Now we're talking. Is she single?
She's divorced.
Even better.
Mickey, why is the little girl piece holding a paintbrush?
Kids like to paint.
Pumpkin, come play! When this hits, I'm buying you that art studio you always wanted.
Hundred percent off.
What's that mean?
It's a teacher thing. Like a gold star, but for dads.
And none of this happens without my executive producer, Mar—
Velous Ted! Marvelous, marvelous Ted.
Ted's producing?
Well, a board game is just architecture you can fold.

scenes.summary: Three hours later. Ted has mapped the board: no road reaches the school, every road leads back to the dog track. Lily: that tracks. She says goodnight. Mickey, quietly: it's a prototype.

beats.line: Three hours later, nobody was any closer to that school.
I have passed the dog track eleven times, Mickey!
Same. Pretty sure I own a greyhound now.
Because nobody can win. I've mapped every route on this board. Not one of them reaches the school.
Sure they do. Past the bowling alley, through the bar, and then—
And then back to the dog track. Every road leads to the dog track.
It's a perfect closed loop. Like an Escher staircase, but for gambling.
Yeah. That tracks.
Night, Dad.
It's a prototype.

scenes.summary: Mickey has gone, Lily is in the bedroom. Ted, Robin and Barney corner Marshall over Marvelous Ted. He confesses: $1,500, from the studio envelope. He'll replace it by fall. Lily, offscreen: the landlord called, she got the studio, deposit tomorrow. Freeze on Marshall.

beats.line: Marvelous Ted?
I invested in Pick-Up.
Marshall. That is the most irresponsible thing you've ever done. I've never been prouder.
How much?
Fifteen hundred. From the envelope.
The studio envelope?
You're dead. They're never going to find all of you.
It's fine. She's not looking at studios till fall. I'll have it back by then.
Marshall! The landlord called back! I got the studio! I'm putting the deposit down tomorrow!
Marshall had fourteen hours to find fifteen hundred dollars.

scenes.summary: Marshall asks Barney for $1,500 by lunch. Barney will pay it, for one slap. Then two thousand. Marshall refuses: some things are more important than money. Like your marriage? Sure. Let's say marriage.

beats.line: Barney, I need fifteen hundred dollars by lunch. No questions.
Done.
Really?
In exchange for one slap. Fifteen hundred, cash, and that slap goes away forever.
Barney, a slap is not a commodity. It's a sacred trust between a man and your face.
Two thousand.
Make it three thousand, and you can—
Done!
No! Some things are more important than money.
Like your marriage?
Sure. Let's say marriage.

scenes.summary: Lily opens the studio envelope: an IOU from Dad, with a P.S. Don't be mad at Marshall. Marshall walks in cheerfully. The fight: the hopeful eyebrows, her name on the box. Lily won't watch for him at a gate again, not even a game store gate. She leaves. Quiet ending.

beats.line: I've got a studio, with a window and a sink.
I owe you fifteen hundred dollars. Love, Dad.
P.S. Don't be mad at Marshall.
Hey, Lilypad! You haven't opened your envelope yet, right?
You gave my studio to my father.
I gave your studio to a dream.
That's worse! His dreams are where money goes to die!
He had the eyebrows, Lily. The hopeful eyebrows.
I know the eyebrows! I've been saying no to those eyebrows since I had teeth!
He said he wants you to see your name on the box.
Don't.
Lilypad, maybe this time—
I watched a school gate for six years, waiting for him to come around the corner.
I'm not doing it again at a game store.

scenes.label: Saturday, 3:02 PM
scenes.summary: The launch at Dot's Games and Melons. Dot reads from her binder of rejected Mickey games. The door chimes: Mickey hopes it's Lily; it's Barney (doorbell runner 1). Mickey insists she's just running late. Robin, who sees him watching the door, steps away from the game and calls Lily: the duck. He looks at the door every time the bell rings.

beats.line: Fifty-one games, Mickey. I've turned down every one. I keep them in a binder.
Number twelve. Chutes and Lawsuits.
Number thirty-eight. Sorry, Pumpkin. Like Sorry, but every card is an excuse.
Thirty-eight was ahead of its time.
Can I ask why a game store sells cantaloupe?
Cantaloupe pays the rent. Games are my heartbreak.
Pumpkin?
Close. Better dressed.
Mickey, I don't think she's coming.
She'll come. She's just running late.
Hey. Before you hang up, he didn't ask me to call.
Robin, if this is about my dad—
When I was eleven, my dad skipped my hockey final to go duck hunting. He sent me the duck.
A picture of the duck?
The duck, Lily.
I'm not telling you to come. I'm just telling you, every time that bell rings, he looks at the door.
Bye, Robin.

scenes.summary: Lily alone with the IOU. She puts it down, stands, and goes. No lines.

scenes.label: 3:31 PM
scenes.summary: The bell: Mickey says Lily; it's Renee (doorbell runner 2), late for her son's pickup and in need of a present. Barney sells her Pick-Up: in this game, being late is the dog track's fault. Mickey's first sale in fifty-two games. Renee leaves Barney her number. It is a dating game.

beats.line: Lily!
Renee.
I need a present for an eight-year-old, and I have to be at his school in fourteen minutes.
Ma'am. Have you ever played Pick-Up?
Every day at a quarter to four. I'm losing right now.
Then you'll love this. In this game, being late is never your fault.
Whose fault is it?
Ma'am, it's always the dog track.
Sold. Can you wrap it?
Fifty-two games. You're my first sale.
Here's my number. Call after eight. Before eight, I'm a mom.
Mickey. It is a dating game.
I knew it'd find its audience.

scenes.label: 3:40 PM
scenes.summary: The bell again. This time Mickey doesn't turn. It's Lily. She stood across the street for twenty minutes. Every time the bell rang: it's the worst, right? Mickey admits he came to her school once, at 3:40, saw her painting the sidewalk with puddle water, and kept driving. I wasn't fine. He knows; he figured it out around 3:15. Thursday, 3:15, he'll be there: do the discount. Ninety percent off (runner twist).

beats.line: Hey, Dad.
Pumpkin. You came.
I'm late.
Forty minutes. Not that I was counting.
I stood across the street for twenty of them.
Every time that bell rang, I thought—
Yeah. It's the worst, right?
It's the worst.
I came once, you know. To your school. About 3:40.
You did not.
You were painting the sidewalk with puddle water. You looked fine. So I kept driving.
I wasn't fine.
I know. I figured it out today. Around 3:15.
Thursday. 3:15. I'll be at your school. Go ahead. Do the discount.
Ninety percent off.
Ninety! I'm up ten!
Ted. That's practically retail.

scenes.label: 9:48 PM
scenes.summary: Hours after closing, all seven are still playing an unwinnable game. Robin won't let anyone leave until someone reaches the school. Mickey pitches a sequel; Marshall says no; Lily kisses him. The kids: did he show up Thursday? Wednesday. Lily was there anyway, waiting with somebody's kid, so Mickey waited too. He came every Wednesday that year, never won a hand, and that's how Lily got her studio.

beats.line: Mickey. I closed four hours ago.
Nobody leaves until somebody reaches that school.
Robin, I've proven it's impossible. I drew you a diagram.
It's after eight. I have a call to make.
Marshall. Sequel idea. Pick-Up Two: Detention.
No.
So did he actually show up on Thursday?
He showed up Wednesday.
So she should've stuck with a hundred percent.
Lily was there anyway. Somebody's dad is always late, and she always waits with the kid. So Mickey waited too.
Did he ever win a hand?
Not once. A dollar a hand, every Wednesday for a year. That's how Lily got her studio.
